fleet.name: Voyager 1
fleet.power: 3 Multi-Hundred Watt Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (MHW-RTGs) stacked in a series on a boom, producing about 158 We each, at launch.
fleet.where: As of Aug. 21, 2024, Voyager 1 was 164.7 AU from Earth — the farthest object created by humans — moving at a velocity of 38,026.79 mph (17.0 km/second) relative to the Sun.
fleet.desc: Voyager 1 was the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere, the boundary where the influences from outside our solar system are stronger than those from our Sun.
fleet.status: Now, more than 49 years into its mission, Voyager 1 has reached another unprecedented milestone — a distance one light-day away from Earth.
fleet.instrumentStatus: Voyager Spacecraft page (2026-11-16): cosmic ray telescope “Off to save power (Feb. 25, 2025)”, low-energy charged particles “Off to save power (April 17, 2026)”, magnetometer and plasma waves “On”. The Voyager 1 page (2026-11-24) still lists four still-functioning instruments.

fleet.name: Voyager 2
fleet.power: Power was provided by three plutonium oxide radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) mounted at the end of a boom.
fleet.where: Jan 24, 1986: Uranus Flyby / Aug 25, 1989: Neptune Flyby / Nov 25, 2018: Entered Interstellar Space
fleet.desc: Each of the two spacecraft was equipped with a slow-scan color TV camera to take images of the planets and their moons and each also carried an extensive suite of instruments to record magnetic, atmospheric, lunar, and other data about the planetary systems.

fleet.name: Pioneer 10
fleet.power: …the first to use all-nuclear electrical power (two SNAP-19 radioisotope thermal generators [RTGs] capable of delivering about 140 W during the Jupiter encounter).
fleet.where: Pioneer 10 sent its last signal to Earth in January 2003 from a distance of 7.6 billion miles (12.23 billion kilometers).
fleet.desc: First spacecraft placed on a trajectory to escape the solar system into interstellar space

fleet.name: Pioneer 11
fleet.power: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (no wattage on the NASA page)
fleet.where: NASA Ames Research Center made last contact with the spacecraft on Sept. 30, 1995, when Pioneer 11 was 44.1 AU from Earth.
fleet.desc: NASA's Pioneer 11, a sister spacecraft to Pioneer 10, was the first spacecraft to study Saturn up close. The mission ended in 1995 and Pioneer 11 is on a trajectory to take it out of the solar system.

fleet.name: Cassini
fleet.power: Three radioisotope thermoelectric generators – commonly referred to as RTGs – provided power for the spacecraft, including the instruments, computers, and radio transmitters on board, attitude thrusters, and reaction wheels.
fleet.where: On Sept. 15, 2017, the spacecraft made its final approach to the giant planet. This time, Cassini dived into the planet's atmosphere, sending science data for as long as its small thrusters could keep the spacecraft's antenna pointed at Earth.
fleet.desc: It became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, beginning a mission that yielded troves of new insights over more than a decade.
kit: cameras, spectrometers, radar and radio (remote sensing)
magnetic fields, mass, electrical charges and densities of atomic particles (fields and particles)
fleet.numbers: 635 GB science data collected · 294 orbits completed · 453,048 images taken

fleet.name: New Horizons
fleet.power: …a cylindrical radioisotope thermoelectric generator (a spare from the Cassini mission) that provided about 250 watts of power at launch (decaying to 200 watts by the time of the Pluto encounter).
fleet.where: Oct. 1, 2024: New Horizons passed 60 times as far from the Sun as Earth is, meaning the spacecraft is twice as far out as Pluto was when New Horizons flew by on July 14, 2015.
fleet.desc: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft was the first spacecraft to explore Pluto up close, flying by the dwarf planet and its moons on July 14, 2015.

fleet.name: International Space Station
fleet.power: 8 solar arrays provide 75 to 90 kilowatts of power
fleet.where: An international crew of seven people live and work while traveling at a speed of five miles per second, orbiting Earth about every 90 minutes.
fleet.desc: The space station has been continuously occupied since November 2000.
kit: More than 50 computers control the systems on the space station.
On-orbit software monitors approximately 350,000 sensors, ensuring station and crew health and safety.

fleet.name: Hubble Space Telescope
fleet.massNote: about 10,800 kg at launch; about 12,200 kg after the 2009 servicing mission
fleet.power: two 8 x 24.75-foot (2.44 x 7.54-meter) gallium-arsenide solar panels; Power Generation (in sunlight) about 5,500 watts
fleet.where: Low-Earth Orbit altitude of about 300 miles (261 nautical miles, or 483 km), inclined 28.5 degrees to the equator
fleet.desc: Orbiting 300 miles (483 km) above Earth's surface, Hubble avoids the distorting effects of our atmosphere, enabling its clear vision of the cosmos.
fleet.disagree: NASA's Webb fact sheet (2026) says “Hubble orbits 560 kilometers above the Earth”; Hubble by the Numbers gives “> 5,200 watts” for the arrays (data as of 1 March 2024).

fleet.name: James Webb Space Telescope
fleet.massNote: Approx 6200 kg, including observatory, on-orbit consumables and launch vehicle adaptor
fleet.power: The Electrical Power Subsystem converts sunlight shining on the solar array panels into the power needed to operate the other subsystems in the bus as well as the Science Instrument Payload.
fleet.where: 1.5 million km from Earth orbiting the L2 Point
fleet.desc: Webb is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide.

fleet.name: Perseverance (Mars 2020)
fleet.power: Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (MMRTG): About 110 watts at launch, declining a few percent per year
fleet.where: On Oct. 11, its odometer reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), rolling past the record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) by NASA's Opportunity rover (2004-2018).
fleet.desc: Since it landed on the Red Planet in 2021 to search for signs of ancient life, NASA's Perseverance Mars rover has driven farther, faster than any vehicle ever has on the surface of another world.

fleet.name: GPS satellites
fleet.launch: Block IIR 1997–2004; IIF 2010–2016; GPS III from 2018
fleet.where: GPS satellites fly in medium Earth orbit (MEO) at an altitude of approximately 20,200 km (12,550 miles). Each satellite circles the Earth twice a day.
fleet.desc: The GPS space segment consists of a constellation of satellites transmitting radio signals to users.

fleet.name: Landsat 9
fleet.power: (not given on the USGS or NASA pages)
fleet.where: Orbits the Earth in a sun-synchronous, near-polar orbit (98.2 degrees inclination); Achieved an altitude of 705 km (438 mi); Completes one Earth orbit every 99 minutes
fleet.desc: The satellite carries two science instruments, the Operational Land Imager (OLI) and the Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS).
fleet.disagree: USGS: “Landsat 9 collects as many as 750 scenes per day”; NASA: “Landsat 9 collects 740 scenes each day”.

rocket.note: Initially, the full mass of the rocket mf contains the empty mass and all of the propellant at lift off. At the end of the burn, the mass of the rocket contains only the empty mass
rocket.ispWhy: The engine with the higher specific impulse is more efficient because it produces more thrust for the same amount of propellant.

example.quote: Putting these values into the ideal rocket equation, the resulting mass flow ratio MR is equal to 10. From the ideal rocket equation, 90% of the weight of a rocket going to orbit is propellant weight.

rocket.gravity: If you include the effects of gravity in the rocket equation, the equation becomes: Δu = Veq ln(MR) − g0·tb where tb is the time for the burn.

orbit.quote: as the height above the planet increases, the velocity needed to maintain an orbit decreases. A spacecraft flying at a lower orbit must travel faster than a spacecraft flying at a higher orbit.

moulton.escapeWhere: p. 47, read on the page image
moulton.escapeQuote: it is found that V = 11,180 meters, or about 6.95 miles, per sec.
moulton.kepler: the squares of the periodic times of the planets are proportional to the cubes of their mean distances.

hohmann.quote: The desired orbit's perihelion (closest approach to the Sun) will be at the distance of Earth's orbit, and the aphelion (farthest distance from the Sun) will be at the distance of Mars' orbit. This is called a Hohmann Transfer orbit.
hohmann.window: The opportunity to launch a spacecraft on a minimum-energy transfer orbit to Mars occurs about every 25 months.

rtg.quote: A Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator, or RTG, is a type of power system for space missions that converts heat from the natural radioactive decay of plutonium-238 into electricity using devices called thermocouples, where heat is applied across a circuit that includes dissimilar metals. This produces an electric current via the Seebeck effect. This process involves no moving parts.

halfLife.quote: The 87.7-year half-life of 238Pu makes it an excellent heat source for space applications.

voyager.quote2023: Status: As of 2023, the twin Voyagers' RTGs are in stable operation at 225 We.
voyager.loads: As the electrical power decreases, power loads on the spacecraft must be turned off in order to avoid having demand exceed supply.
voyager.rate: The radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG) on each spacecraft puts out 4 watts less each year.

solar.quote: One of the major SORCE contributions was to establish a more accurate value at 1361 Wm-2, which leads to 340 W m-2 for the globally averaged solar input to Earth.
solar.juno: Jupiter’s orbit is five times farther from the sun than Earth’s location, so the giant planet receives about 25 times less sunlight than Earth.

link.quote: If the power were radiated isotropically, the power flux density at the receiver ρ would be the transmitted power divided by the area of a sphere of radius r.
link.bsfGain: Voyager's, HGA, for example, provides a gain of 47 dBi at X-band.

voyager.quote: Uplink communications is via S-band (16-bits/sec command rate) while an X-band transmitter provides downlink telemetry at 160 bits/sec normally and 1.4 kbps for playback of high-rate plasma wave data. All data are transmitted from and received at the spacecraft via the 3.7 meter high-gain antenna (HGA).

dsn.quote: Each Deep Space Network site has one huge, 230-foot (70-meter) diameter antenna, one 85-foot (26-meter) diameter antenna, and multiple 112-foot (34-meter) diameter antennas capable of tracking spacecraft traveling tens of billions of miles from Earth.

weak.quote: The antennas must capture Voyager information from a signal so weak that the power striking the antenna is only 10 exponent -16 watts (1 part in 10 quadrillion).
By the time those signals reach Earth, they're one-tenth of a billionth-trillionth of a watt.

attitude.wheels: Hubble relies on its complement of four 100-pound (45 kg) reaction wheel assemblies for attitude control, and four magnetic torque bars for momentum management.
attitude.newton: If one of the reaction wheels turns clockwise, Hubble will turn counterclockwise. Changing the spin speed of any of the wheels produces a rotational force called torque.
attitude.gyro: Hubble's gyroscopes spin at 19,200 revolutions per minute.
attitude.slow: However, at its fastest, Hubble only moves as quickly as the minute hand of a clock (approximately 90 degrees in 15 minutes).
attitude.bsf: They provide a means to trade angular momentum back and forth between spacecraft and wheels. To rotate the vehicle in one direction, you spin up the proper wheel in the opposite direction. To rotate the vehicle back, you slow down the wheel.

thermal.balance: qsolar + qalbedo + qplanetshine + Qgen = Qstored + Qout,rad
thermal.quote: Spacecraft temperatures are determined by how much heat is absorbed, stored, generated, and dissipated by the spacecraft.
thermal.radiator: A radiator is a dedicated surface for dissipating excess heat via radiative heat transfer and has a high IR emissivity and low solar absorptivity—an optical property combination typically referred to as “radiator properties.”

sb.quote: The total radiation emitted by a blackbody is proportional to the radiating surface area and the fourth power of its absolute temperature. The proportionality constant, σ, equals 5.670374419 x 10-8 watts per square meter x K-4.

thermal.louvers: The louvers are positioned by bi-metallic strips similar to those in a thermostat. They directly force the louvers open when internal temperatures are high, permitting heat to radiate into space.

instruments.q: Spectroscopic instruments are optical remote-sensing instruments that split the light received from their targets into component wavelengths for measuring and analyzing.

Light falling on a well is absorbed by a photoconductive substrate such as silicon and releases a quantity of electrons proportional to the intensity of light. The CCD detects and stores accumulated electrical charge representing the light level on each well over time. These charges are read out for conversion to digital data.
Magnetometers are direct-sensing instruments that detect and measure the interplanetary and solar magnetic fields in the vicinity of the spacecraft.

An instrument that quantitatively measures the intensity of electromagnetic radiation in some bands within the spectrum. A radiometer is usually further identified by the portion of the spectrum it covers; for example, visible, infrared, or microwave bands.

An active radar instrument, whether aboard a space-based platform or aboard an aircraft, emits microwave radiation in a series of pulses from an antenna. When the energy reaches the target, some of the energy is reflected back toward the instrument. This backscattered microwave radiation is detected, measured, and timed.
Distance to the object is determined by recording the time between transmitted and backscattered pulses and by using the speed of light to calculate the distance traveled.

High-energy particle detector instruments measure the energy spectra of trapped energetic electrons, and the energy and composition of atomic nuclei. They may employ several independent solid-state-detector telescopes.

Plasma detectors serve the low-end of particle energies. They measure the density, composition, temperature, velocity and three-dimensional distribution of plasmas, which are soups of positive ions and electrons
Mass Spectrometers, for example the Cassini Spacecraft's INMS, Ion and Neutral Mass Spectrometer, report the species of atoms or molecules that enter the instrument.
By studying the radio waves originating from these sources, astronomers can learn about their composition, structure, and motion.

chain.q: An imaging instrument uses optics such as lenses or mirrors to project an image onto a detector, where it is converted to digital data.
Landsat 9 improvements include higher radiometric resolution for OLI (14-bit quantization increased from 12-bits for Landsat 8) … Landsat 9 can differentiate 16,384 shades of a given wavelength.

Telemetry data from science instruments and engineering subsystems is picked up by the CDS, where it is assembled into packages appropriate to the telemetry frame or packet scheme in use (for example CCSDS).
The storage devices can be commanded to play out their stored data for downlink when DSN resources are available, and then to overwrite the old data with new.
A 20-Watt transmitter using a 47-dBi gain HGA would have an effective power of a megawatt along the highly directional beam.

The three Deep Space Network complexes are located at Goldstone, near Barstow, California; near Madrid, Spain; and near Canberra, Australia. The strategic placement of these sites permits constant communication with spacecraft as our planet rotates
The DSN Downlink Tracking & Telemetry subsystem recreates the spacecraft's digital data bit for bit by recognizing the downlinked symbols and decoding them.
All data are processed to at least a Level 1, but most have associated Level 2 (derived geophysical variables) and Level 3 (variables mapped on uniform space-time grid scales) products.

bottleneck.q: The download of the entire set of data collected during the encounter with Pluto and Charon – about 6.25 gigabytes – took over 15 months and was officially completed at 21:48 UT on Oct. 25, 2016. Such a lengthy period was necessary because the spacecraft was roughly 4.5 light-hours from Earth and it could only transmit 1-2 kilobits per second.
